gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the inverter itself uses power while it sits idle: Inverter Geek measured the Sun Gold Power SPH6548P drawing 50–80 W continuously just to stay on. That is 1.2–1.9 kWh a day, or 23–38% of a single 5.12 kWh 51.2 V 100 Ah battery, used up before any appliance runs. ChatGPT's own '4,500 Wh ÷ 300 W = 15 hours' therefore comes out at about 11.8–12.9 hours.
standout_why: ChatGPT's search for this query came back empty in both saved chats, so there were no cited rival pages or top results to compare against. I compared against ChatGPT's two answers instead. Both runtime calculators (4,500 Wh ÷ 300 W = 15 h, and 10 kWh at 500 W = 14.4 h) allow only for 90% inverter efficiency and 80–90% usable capacity. Neither counts the inverter's fixed idle draw. That draw matters most at the low essential loads (fridge, Wi-Fi, lights) that both answers lead with, and it pushes the shopper from one 51.2 V 100 Ah module toward two. I scored it 2 rather than 3 because I could not open the battery's own discharge-current spec, which is the second half of the 'two modules' argument.
kit_items: Inverter/charger: Sun Gold Power SPH6548P 6.5 kW 48 V split-phase hybrid. It does 120/240 V, has 2 MPPTs and charges at up to 140 A, and the maker's page says it talks CAN/RS485 to SunGoldPower batteries. It matches the '48V-class + split-phase inverter/charger' design ChatGPT described, and the inverter and battery can go in one cart.

Battery: 2× Sun Gold Power SG48100P 51.2 V 100 Ah server-rack LiFePO4 (UL1973/UL9540A), 10.24 kWh total. With an 80 W idle draw, one 5.12 kWh module gives up 37.5% of its energy per day to overhead (80 W × 24 h = 1,920 Wh). With two modules that falls to 18.75%. At 300 W plus 80 W idle, 10,240 Wh ÷ 380 W ≈ 27 h on nominal capacity, against about 13.5 h with one module.
Not in the cart: a listed transfer switch or subpanel and an electrician for the panel connection, which ChatGPT already flagged. DC fusing and cabling sized for the inverter's battery current.

findings.label: ChatGPT's runtime example corrected for idle draw
findings.note: Uses ChatGPT's own 4,500 Wh usable and 300 W load: 4,500 ÷ (300 + 80) = 11.8 h and 4,500 ÷ (300 + 50) = 12.9 h. At a 100 W overnight load (router, lights, fridge cycling off): 4,500 ÷ (100 + 80) = 25 h, not 45 h. The lighter the load, the larger the share lost to idle.
